references.text: Isaiah prophesies that the Lord's servants will eat, but those who forsake the Lord will go hungry; the Lord's servants will rejoice, but the others will weep – a direct parallel to the reversal of fullness into hunger and laughter into sorrow.
Proverbs teaches that even under laughter the heart may have sorrow, and joy can end in grief – a wisdom saying that mirrors the warning that laughter now will turn to sorrow.
James exhorts: "Wail and mourn and weep! Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom." This is a close parallel to Jesus' woe over those who laugh now.
The beatitude in Luke 6:21 is the direct opposite: "Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh" – a contrast to the woe pronounced on those who laugh now.

Babylon says of herself that she sits as queen and will never see sorrow, but in one day her plagues will come – death, mourning, and famine. An example of how self-satisfied abundance is turned into suffering.
Amos pronounces woe on those who live in luxury and security in Zion, who eat, drink, and make merry without caring about the ruin of their people – they will be the first to go into exile.
Isaiah pronounces woe on those who chase after wine and feasting, and do not regard the work of the Lord – a parallel to the woe over those who are full and satisfied now.

In the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, Abraham says: "Remember that you received your good things during your lifetime, while Lazarus received evil things. Now he is comforted here, but you are in torment." A reversal of earthly abundance into eternal suffering.
Jesus' beatitude for those who mourn, "for they shall be comforted", stands in contrast to the woe over those who laugh now, for they will mourn and weep.
